definition: Implied weight is read from the ratio between a character's visible exerted effort (strain, bracing, visible force) and the resulting effect (how far the object or the character's own body actually displaces) — high effort with a small effect reads as heavy, low effort with a large effect reads as light, independent of the object's stated size or the rig's actual mass.
purpose: Give an animator a deliberate, adjustable dial for selling an object's weight through the character's performance, usable even on a rig with no physical mass or simulation behind it.
visible_effect: A character straining hard (bracing, leaning, visible tension) while the object barely moves reads as struggling with something heavy; a character exerting minimal visible force while producing large displacement reads as handling something light, even where the two clips use the same object model.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Lets a viewer judge an object's weight from the performer's relationship to it alone, without needing to know the object's real mass — the presenter's own framing: 5% effort producing 100% effect reads as light, 80% effort producing 5% effect reads as a heavy struggle.
physical_interpretation: Not a physical simulation — a deliberately exaggerated performance convention standing in for a force/resistance relationship a rig with no mass model cannot compute.
use_cases: any shot where a character interacts with an object whose weight must read correctly and the object itself carries no simulated mass

escalating a repeated failed attempt — the presenter's stated rule that a character should not repeat the identical effort level on a second try; a failed push should be followed by a visibly different, more intense attempt, not the same motion looped
non_use_cases: an object whose weight is already sold structurally (a visible mechanism, a stated in-fiction weight, a physics-simulated prop) where an exaggerated effort read would contradict the established behaviour

a single instantaneous effect with no visible ongoing exertion to compare against (a thrown object already in flight) — the ratio needs both a visible effort phase and a visible effect phase to compare
interactions: weight_then_strength_formula (W02, video 19) — a two-beat structure (establish resistance, then overcome it); this entry is the continuous ratio read moment-to-moment throughout a struggle, not only at its two beats — compatible descriptions of the same struggle at different grains

layered_anticipation (W01, video 1) — the presenter's "we don't retry in the same way" rule is a specific application of escalating intensity across repeated sub-phases before a resolution, the same shape layered_anticipation already names for a single wind-up
cadence_representation: Not computed. Effort has no representation at all (it would require reading strain or bracing from a pose, which is not attempted anywhere); effect is measurable today as a displacement magnitude (`ai/motion.js sampleMotion` position/linear_velocity over the interaction phase), but nothing divides one by the other or calls the ratio a weight signal.
control_surface: None for effort. `sample_motion` already returns the effect half (displacement/velocity) for any item and range.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Effect half — real: total displacement or peak `linear_velocity` of the manipulated object (or the character's own root, for a self-directed struggle) across a declared interaction phase, from `ai/motion.js sampleMotion`. Effort half — not measurable in this build: there is no pose-strain or muscular-tension measure, so the numerator of the stated ratio cannot be computed, only the denominator. Reporting a ratio would need a declared or authored effort LEVEL as input, not a measurement of effort from the pose.
failure_modes: an object read as heavy by its model or story context, animated with low visible effort and large easy displacement — the effort/effect mismatch reads as the object being light regardless of its stated size
repeating an identical failed attempt at the same effort level rather than escalating, which reads as the character not learning from the failure rather than as a struggle building
examples: presenter's own framing: "if I put in five percent effort and I get a hundred percent effect, is that a heavy object" versus "if I put in eighty percent of my effort and I get five percent effect, does that look like a heavy object that I'm struggling with" — video @ 02:18-02:53
the retry rule: "we don't retry in the same way... if it doesn't work then I'm going to try harder, I'm going to try something different... more intensity" — video @ 03:10-03:29
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/0x9f21vFqcE @ 02:00-03:32 — stated directly by the AnimSchool instructor as a named authored system ("effort versus effect is a system that I came up with"), not a citation of a written source; experimental until validated
